title: Fifteen Probationers and a Compromise: St Thomas', July 1860
dek: After years of delay, the Nightingale Fund accepted St Thomas' Hospital's terms, and in July 1860 the first fifteen probationers began a year's training under its matron.

story.company: Nightingale Training School for Nurses (later Florence Nightingale Faculty of Nursing, King's College London)
story.event: Accepting St Thomas' Hospital's terms and opening the nurse training school with fifteen probationers
story.summary: The Nightingale Fund, raised by public subscription from November 1855, was placed with St Thomas' Hospital in 1860 after long delay; by the historian Monica Baly's account the hospital insisted its matron, Sarah Wardroper, be superintendent and the resident medical officer pared back Nightingale's plan. The first fifteen probationers arrived on 9 July 1860 for a one-year course paid at £10 with board and lodging. Early sickness and dismissal rates were high; by 1900 the Fund had trained 1,020 nurses.
paragraphs: On 9 July 1860, according to hospital records held in the London Archives, fifteen women arrived at St Thomas' Hospital in Southwark as the first probationers of a new training school for nurses. Florence Nightingale's name was on the fund that paid for them, but she did not run the school. The hospital's matron, Sarah Wardroper, did.

The money had waited a long time. A public meeting in London on 9 November 1855 had launched a subscription in gratitude for Nightingale's Crimean War work, and about £44,000 came in. She wanted it spent on training nurses. Before she took to her bed, the nursing historian Monica Baly later wrote, she claimed to have visited every hospital in London. She liked King's College Hospital but was wary of its religious order, and other hospitals were considered; not all of them, Baly suggested, wanted the famous fund in their house.

St Thomas' took it, on its own terms. In Baly's account, the governors insisted that their matron become superintendent, and in spring 1859 the resident medical officer, R. G. Whitfield, pared back Nightingale's ambitious plan, declaring that "the probationers would not understand the half that you intend." The archive tells it more warmly: Nightingale was drawn to St Thomas' because Wardroper had begun reforming it in 1855. Either way, after three years, Baly wrote, the Fund Council took the best deal it could get. In March 1860 it wrote formally to the governors proposing the school.

The terms were plain. Each probationer received £10 for the year, with board, lodging, a uniform and an allowance of tea and sugar. Teaching was mostly supervised work on the wards. Wardroper could dismiss anyone at any time, and those approved at the end were entered on a register of certified nurses and found posts, having agreed to serve on in hospitals for the poor. Baly called it a servant's contract.

The start was slow. Sickness and dismissals ran so high, Baly found, that there was hardly anyone to send to the hospitals asking for Nightingale nurses. Still, the archive records, a first group went to Liverpool within two years, and later groups reached Canada and Australia. By Baly's count the fund had trained 1,020 nurses by 1900, about 25 a year.

quote.text: Let no man think lightly of evil, saying in his heart, It will not come nigh unto me. Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the fool becomes full of evil, even if he gather it little by little.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: The verse is about evil, but its arithmetic fits any habit. The school's good filled slowly, about 25 nurses a year. By Baly's account so did the cost of its first concessions, such as the matron's sweeping authority, which Nightingale later regretted. Both pots were filling at once.

reflection: Nightingale did not get the school she first designed. She got the one a hospital would agree to, run by its own matron, and the fund's council let it open rather than go on waiting. Some of what was conceded did harm later. Some of it simply got the first fifteen women through the door.

You will make deals like this too, with a partner, a funder or your own energy in a hard week. Taking the half that is on offer is often right. What helps is writing down, at the time, what you gave up, so you can come back to it on purpose instead of finding it years later.
invitation: Think of one compromise you accepted to get something started. Write a single line saying what you gave up, and put a date beside it for when you will look at it again.

cross_checks.claim: A public subscription launched in November 1855 raised about £44,000-£45,000 for Nightingale to use on nurse training.
The first probationers began training at St Thomas' in summer 1860 (9 July by the hospital records), with the matron Sarah Wardroper as superintendent.
Probationers were paid £10 for a one-year course with board and lodging, and approved nurses were registered and found posts.
The school was placed at St Thomas' only after a long delay, on terms that made the hospital's own matron its head.

research_notes: Why St Thomas': sources disagree. The London Archives' catalogue says Nightingale was attracted to St Thomas' because Wardroper had begun reforms in 1855, and Wikipedia's Wardroper article (citing Lynn McDonald's edition of Nightingale's writings on the school) says she chose it largely for Wardroper and Whitfield; Monica Baly (1984), working from the British Library and St Thomas' records, argued that Nightingale hardly knew Wardroper, that the governors made their matron's appointment a condition, and that Whitfield watered down the plan in 1859. The story gives Baly's account and the archive's side by side and does not settle it. Fund total: £44,000 (archive), £44,039 by June 1856 (Wikipedia), some £45,000 (Baly; Stewart), nearly £50,000 (Guy's and St Thomas'); the story says about £44,000. Opening date: the archive and Wikipedia give 9 July 1860; Stewart says the course was due to begin on 24 June 1860, and a 1960 centenary report called the date uncertain; the story gives 9 July as the hospital records' date. Length of later service: Baly says probationers agreed to four further years in hospitals for the poor, Stewart says at least three; the story gives no number. Baly says Nightingale was 'not greatly interested' in the school's first years at the Surrey Gardens site (1862-71), having more urgent business; the story says only that she did not run it. The 1,020 nurses trained by 1900 and the high sickness and dismissal rates are Baly's figures and are attributed to her; the Liverpool group within two years is the archive's statement. Baly's article is printed as page PDFs (pp. 2-7) linked from the cited landing page; pages 2 to 6 were read in full (page 7, the notes, would not load). Whitfield's remark is quoted as Baly prints it, citing her note 7. The Dhammapada verse is about evil; it is applied by analogy to habits formed by early concessions, and the connection says so.
